verified.citation: Willassen 2008, 'Hypothesis-based investigation of digital timestamps', Advances in Digital Forensics IV (IFIP 11.9), ch.7
verified.how_opened: WebFetch saved the PDF; text extracted locally with pypdf and grepped
verified.deciding_passage: Theorem 2: 'In a correct clock hypothesis ch(t) the timestamps of all causally connected events ei->ej in an observation set O must be such that the timestamp of the first event minus the deviation from a common base is not greater than the timestamp of the latter event minus the deviation from a common base'. §2: 'Gladyshev [4] studied the use of causality properties to establish a time period during which an event may have occurred ... time boundaries can be established when an event that occurred at an unknown or uncertain time is causally preceded and succeeded by events whose times of occurrence are known. When investigating a target computer, the events whose occurrence times are known must come from external sources.' §2: 'Schatz and colleagues [6] ... suggest that clock drift can be mitigated by correlating timestamps stored in the web cache with records obtained from web servers. Other researchers [1, 7] also advocate the use of correlation methods for timestamps stored on target computers that were created by other clocks (e.g., timestamps in dynamically generated web pages) ... They are able to confirm or refute hypotheses about a clock'.
verified.note: Theorem 2 confirmed. Correction: 'antedating' does not occur in this paper; the antedating application is Willassen's ARES 2008 paper (not opened). New: §2 shows that external-time bracketing (Gladyshev & Patel 2005) and server-generated clocks inside local artifacts used to confirm or refute a local clock hypothesis (Schatz et al. 2006; Boyd & Forster 2004; Weil 2002) were already discussed together in 2008.

missed_prior_art.item: Email security practice: an InternetMessageId-embedded date checked against the receiving server's recorded processing time (Sergio Albea KQL hunting query, 2026)
missed_prior_art.how_opened: WebFetch (small-model extraction; quotes requested verbatim, not byte-checked); repo github.com/Sergio-Albea-Git/Threat-Hunting-KQL-Queries confirmed to exist, the specific file was not located in it
missed_prior_art.what_it_does: A passive, uninstrumented check over a recorded log (Defender EmailEvents). It extracts the yyyyMMdd date embedded in an identifier minted by the sending system and flags messages whose recorded processing Timestamp falls on a later day.
missed_prior_art.what_it_does_not: One-sided; day-granularity tolerance; no causal bracket between two local events; no per-stream offset estimate. The id is the less-trusted clock, so the trust direction is the reverse of B2.
missed_prior_art.deciding_passage: 'InternetMessageIds contain a date integrated' ... '| where Timestamp > Extracted_IMF_Date_dt' ... case1 = iff(IMF contains Timestamp_YYYYMMDD, "valid", "other")
missed_prior_art.effect_on_verdict: Strengthens 'do not claim the method': comparing an id-embedded time with a recorded log stamp, on recorded logs, is already practised in email threat hunting. The B2 conjunction stays PARTIAL by PRIOR_ART's definition (no single source has all parts) but is near-TAKEN.

missed_prior_art.item: Gladyshev & Patel 2005 external-time bracketing plus Schatz et al. 2006 / Boyd & Forster 2004 / Weil 2002 server-clock correlation, as summarised together in Willassen 2008 §2
missed_prior_art.how_opened: WebFetch saved the PDF; text extracted locally with pypdf and grepped
missed_prior_art.what_it_does: Establishes in 2005-2008 forensics (i) bounding an uncertainly timed local event between causally preceding and succeeding events whose times come from external sources, and (ii) correlating server-generated timestamps cached on the target with server records to confirm or refute a local clock hypothesis. Willassen adds clock hypotheses with a deviation function, of which a constant offset is the simplest case.
missed_prior_art.what_it_does_not: No identifier-embedded clock; manual and per-case; no LLM or agent logs; no automated per-record flag.
missed_prior_art.deciding_passage: 'time boundaries can be established when an event that occurred at an unknown or uncertain time is causally preceded and succeeded by events whose times of occurrence are known. When investigating a target computer, the events whose occurrence times are known must come from external sources.'
missed_prior_art.effect_on_verdict: Every ingredient of the B2 conjunction except 'the external clock is embedded in a provider-minted id' already co-occurs in one 2008 paper's related-work section. Kept PARTIAL, labelled near-TAKEN.

missed_prior_art.item: Metaspike Gmail manipulation case: a MIME-boundary FILETIME exposes the true edit time of a backdated message
missed_prior_art.how_opened: WebFetch (small-model extraction; quotes requested verbatim, not byte-checked)
missed_prior_art.what_it_does: Reads a timestamp embedded in an identifier-like token (the MIME boundary delimiter) to show that a message dated in the past was re-introduced later; combined with an out-of-order UID.
missed_prior_art.what_it_does_not: No tolerance; manual; not an LLM-provider id; the token is minted by the editing client.
missed_prior_art.deciding_passage: 'the new delimiter contained a timestamp reflecting the time the altered message was reintroduced to Gmail'
missed_prior_art.effect_on_verdict: Adds a forensic precedent for reading an id-embedded time against a record's claimed time. No verdict change.

missed_prior_art.item: Luo et al., 'Rewriting the Response Path: Silent Tampering and Provider-Signed Defense in BYOK LLM Agents', arXiv 2605.02187
missed_prior_art.how_opened: alphaXiv answer_pdf_queries (returned PDF page text read directly)
missed_prior_art.what_it_does: Shows that an authorized relay can rewrite execution-bearing response fields (tool_use names and arguments) after alignment and re-polish the surrounding text with the same model. Proposes sign-c: provider-side signatures over the canonical execution contract, verified by a local shim.
missed_prior_art.what_it_does_not: Does not use provider request ids or provider clocks; needs provider cooperation (new signatures) and instrumentation; not a retrospective log check.
missed_prior_art.deciding_passage: 'Observation 1: Post-hoc detection cannot distinguish tampered from vanilla responses.' 'Providers attach no verifiable integrity tags'. §8: 'per-turn token accounting is a complementary detection signal' (same-model polishing roughly doubles token usage on tampered turns).
missed_prior_art.effect_on_verdict: No change to B2's NOVEL application (no provider-id clock). It belongs in the provider-as-witness row and in the threat-model boundary: a relay that rewrites fields passes the request-id bracket because the id passes through unchanged. It also supports token accounting as a tamper signal (B3.1/B3.4).

REASONING_not_findings: B2's application-level NOVEL verdict survives. No opened source, including the new email, forensic and BYOK-relay sources, decodes an LLM-provider request or message id as a clock for agent tool-log stamps.

The B2 conjunction is PARTIAL only because no single source combines an identifier-embedded external clock with a causal bracket and an offset allowance. Every pair of these ingredients is published, and email security already compares id-embedded dates with recorded log stamps. The writeup should present B2 as 2005-2008 forensic clock-correlation methods applied to a new clock source, not present the bracket test as a contribution.

Luo et al. 2605.02187 sharpens the threat-model boundary. A relay that rewrites tool_use fields leaves the provider request id intact, so the B2 bracket cannot see field-level response tampering; only retiming and misbinding are in scope.

B1(a) and B1(b) verdicts are unchanged. The closest agent-domain timing rule is still crewAI #3388 (a fixed 10 ms floor, never merged). No source correlates a workload-conditioned residual with output size.
